# Mixed-demo integration and action discipline

Use this class-level review when one Continual-ARC instance presents demonstrations with very different dimensions, palettes, or visible structures, or after an incorrect prediction.

## Workflow
1. Maintain one cross-demo ledger: input/output dimensions, palette roles, separators or motifs, exact input-to-output relation, and unchanged regions. Do not discard an example because it looks unlike the test or earlier demos.
2. After every returned pair, update the ledger and test candidate generators against the complete set before deciding the next action. Avoid demo chains that only accumulate data.
3. Request another demo only for a concrete unresolved distinction: name the competing hypotheses and the feature in a new pair that could discriminate them. Uncertainty alone is not a reason to spend a demo.
4. Treat incorrect feedback as falsifying the proposed generator. Revisit output shape/scope, transformation class, mapping, trigger, and phase. Do not repeat the candidate or submit a cosmetic edit; validate a materially different rule against all demos first.
5. For sparse trajectory candidates, enumerate all plausible seeds, directions, colors, and endpoints separately. Test for simultaneous rays and negative/unchanged examples; do not submit only the most salient ray without cross-demo support.
6. In puzzle turns, emit exactly one action-only JSON object and no prose. Before submission, validate output dimensions, row lengths, and values.

## Pointers
For grid-specific base procedures, use `arc-grid-solving-continual`. Its references `mixed-demo-consistency.md`, `demo-chain-recovery.md`, and `cross-demo-generator-validation.md` provide additional examples. For detailed recovery after a failed trajectory prediction, see the trajectory/error-recovery references.

# Cellwise mask validation across heterogeneous demos

When an ARC task has a distinctive colored seed in noisy grids, do not equate resemblance with the rule. Track the seed shape, eligible target values, and spatial generator as independent hypotheses. For every demo, enumerate the full input/output difference mask and preserve negative evidence: unchanged lookalikes, untouched target-valued cells, and the original seed.

Before another demo or a submission, replay the proposed generator against every pair, especially when seed shape, palette, or dimensions vary. A literal translated-template matcher that looks plausible on one example but fails the varied demos is falsified; do not patch it by shifting a few cells. Request additional examples only for explicit remaining alternatives and a specific discriminating observation.

# Noisy-background motif generators: validation checkpoint

When a demo contains a small colored seed motif in a noisy background and the output extends that color into many background cells, do not infer the generator from visual resemblance alone. Commonly confusable candidates include translated copies, periodic masks, alternating reflected tilings, diagonal/ray propagation, and local matching.

For each demo, record the seed's exact coordinates and bounding box, then enumerate every changed cell and every unchanged background cell. Test each candidate against the complete mask, including phase, boundaries, preserved non-background cells, and repeated seed cells. Cross-check the candidate on differently sized and differently shaped demos before applying it to the test. A wrong submission falsifies the full proposed generator; do not make an unsupported period, phase, or reflection adjustment as a cosmetic retry.

This checklist is a validation procedure, not evidence that any one candidate class is correct for a particular task.

# Seed-motif generator checkpoint after a wrong submission

A salient colored seed embedded in a noisy grid does not by itself imply a copy rule. Candidate classes can include translated shape occurrences, periodic/lattice replication, directional rays, or combinations. Before extrapolating, record the seed's exact coordinates and the complete input/output difference mask in every demo. Verify both positive and negative cases: why each changed cell is selected, and why visually similar unchanged cells are excluded. Check palettes and dimensions that vary across demos; distinguish the seed color, target/background color, and unrelated noise empirically rather than assuming one role from a single pair.

After an incorrect submission, discard the whole generator. Do not move a few cells, swap a presumed background color, or switch to a nearby geometric interpretation without replaying it against every demo. With a costly attempt budget, use remaining demos for explicit competing hypotheses and only submit after a full-mask validation. Preserve all cells outside the supported transformation and verify dimensions/row lengths.

# Noisy seed motif inference

Use alongside `arc-grid-solving-continual` when one compact colored motif appears amid noisy/background cells and the output changes many cells without changing dimensions.

## Workflow
1. Record seed color, exact seed coordinates, normalized shape, background/noise palette, and all cells changed from input to output. Keep shape, target value, and placement generator as separate unknowns.
2. Compare complete masks across every demo. Distinguish whether the output changes the dominant background, minority/noise cells, or only cells satisfying a spatial condition; record untouched lookalikes as negative evidence.
3. Test candidate generators independently: translated motif occurrences, periodic/tiling masks, line/ray propagation, and other position rules supported by geometry. For each, identify which input values are eligible for change; never presume the eligible value is zero.
4. Replay candidates cell-by-cell across every palette and grid size. Reject any candidate that fails even one changed/unchanged cell. Maintain exact original seed cells and unrelated values unless demos show otherwise.
5. After a wrong submission, reject the entire generator. Revisit seed extraction, output scope, eligible background color, and transformation geometry. After two distinct failures, avoid speculative submissions; request a demo only to distinguish explicit remaining alternatives and integrate it before acting.
6. Validate dimensions, row lengths, and values, then emit exactly one permitted action JSON per turn.

## Pitfalls
- A conspicuous seed is not automatically a literal template copied only onto zeros.
- Seed form, changed color, and placement rule can be independent; infer each from the full demos.
- Diverse palettes and shapes are useful cross-validation, not grounds to discard examples.
- Recoloring the right-looking locations with the wrong palette or scope is still a falsified generator.

# Continual-ARC payload validation

Apply alongside the general Continual-ARC inference workflow. Use this checklist whenever producing a grid, especially for long grids or after repeated rejected actions.

## Workflow
1. Infer the transformation from the complete demo ledger; formatting checks never replace rule validation.
2. Before submission, validate mechanically: exactly the intended row count, identical expected width on every row, each cell an integer from 0 through 9, and dimensions within 1–30.
3. Confirm unchanged regions and original markers are preserved unless a demonstrated rule changes them.
4. If a submission is marked invalid, check payload shape first: count every row and inspect every row width, then rebuild a valid payload. Do not interpret malformed-grid feedback as evidence about the transformation.
5. If a valid grid is incorrect, discard the full generator. After repeated distinct failures, stop speculative variants and return to full-diff cross-demo reasoning; request a targeted demo when it could distinguish concrete hypotheses.
6. Keep the exact protocol: one action-only JSON object per turn.

## Pitfalls
- Long arrays are easy to miscount visually; one short or long row invalidates the output.
- A syntactically valid grid can still encode the wrong transformation. Payload validation and hypothesis validation are separate checks.
- Repeated submissions without materially revised cross-demo support consume budget without adding evidence.

# Continual-ARC colored-template occurrence

Use when examples show one distinct colored motif embedded in a noisy two-color grid and the output recolors matching zero/background positions.

## Procedure
1. Extract the full set of coordinates of the distinctive color and normalize to its minimum row and column. Record the exact binary template, including holes and non-rectangular boundaries.
2. Enumerate every translation of that template within the grid. A candidate occurrence is valid when every template coordinate lands on the designated target/background color (typically 0); do not require non-template cells in the bounding box to match unless demos prove this.
3. Replay the occurrence rule against every demo: each reported placement must correspond to newly recolored target cells, and unchanged lookalike regions must be explained. Include translated overlaps and edge placements.
4. Preserve all non-target cells and original colored seed cells. Color only template coordinates at valid occurrences. If a demo shows a different orientation, explicitly test and validate that orientation rather than assuming rotations/reflections.
5. Apply translations to test; validate bounds, dimensions, row widths, and values. Emit exactly one allowed action JSON.

## Pitfalls
- Do not infer regular tiling merely from repeated-looking copies; enumerate translations against the full template mask.
- Do not color the template's entire bounding rectangle—holes are excluded.
- Do not require zeros under template holes to be zero; match only the actual colored-mask coordinates unless evidence demands otherwise.
- Integrate every demo before another request. A large demo budget is not reason to request in a chain without testing candidate placements.

# Sparse trajectory extension in Continual-ARC

Use this as a focused addendum when demos contain a few colored cells that become a longer diagonal, row, column, or ray. Keep the Continual-ARC action protocol and budget discipline from `arc-grid-solving-continual`.

## Procedure
1. Record each relevant non-background input/output coordinate using consistent zero- or one-based indexing. Identify seed/anchor colors and any paired endpoints.
2. Compute coordinate differences across the input markers. Test whether the output adds cells following a constant direction vector, a repeated offset, or a line between anchors.
3. Compare all demos, including differing grid sizes. A short demo may show only one extension step while a larger demo exposes the continuation, so do not infer a fixed extension length from the first pair.
4. Determine scope and stopping behavior from full outputs: whether the ray starts at a specific marker, passes through or skips other cells, stops at a boundary, and what happens where it intersects existing objects. Preserve all unrelated input cells.
5. Project the validated coordinate rule onto the test dimensions and check every generated coordinate is in bounds. Validate output dimensions, values, and unchanged regions.
6. If more than one trajectory rule remains viable, request a demo only when it distinguishes specific alternatives; otherwise avoid costly probing or speculative submissions.

## Pitfalls
- Do not simply copy the visible changed mask from a smaller demo.
- Do not assume one-step extension or a fixed number of added cells based on a short example.
- Do not overwrite existing markers unless demonstrations establish that behavior.
- A wrong submission falsifies the previous generator; revise direction, anchor, or scope materially rather than making a cosmetic coordinate tweak.

## Example lesson
A small demo can show a diagonal extension by one cell, but a much larger demo may reveal that the same trajectory continues repeatedly across the entire grid, with different rays associated with different colored markers. The correct test prediction should be generated from those repeated coordinate relations, not from the short demo's apparent local completion.

# Mixed demo evidence and failed trajectory review

This instance produced five demonstrations with strongly heterogeneous appearances: a short unchanged pair of sparse markers; a large grid with boundary markers and multiple diagonal traces; horizontal/vertical band structures; and a final 30x8 grid where isolated 9 markers caused directional fills. The test had two 9 cells and a pair of 5s at opposing corners. Repeated submissions based on copying color fills or drawing straight/diagonal rays failed, showing that local visual analogies were not enough to establish the shared rule.

## Reusable inference checkpoint
1. Preserve a structured ledger per demo: dimensions, palette roles, every non-background coordinate, exact output changes, and unchanged cells. Record identity pairs as trigger constraints.
2. Compare structural relations across examples, not merely the most salient motif. In particular, identify any repeated corner/boundary pattern or positional relationship that may control the changed region.
3. Keep trigger, selected objects/cells, output geometry, fill color, and path direction separate. A test containing multiple markers does not prove each is an independent ray source.
4. Before spending another demo, name at least two hypotheses and the exact observable that would distinguish them. Do not issue successive requests without integrating the newly returned pair.
5. After any wrong submission, discard the entire generator. A change from horizontal rays to diagonal rays, or adding omitted rays, is not a meaningful revision unless it fits all demos cell by cell.
6. Submit only a complete candidate generated by a rule that explains the heterogeneous examples and validates all output dimensions and values.

This record documents the failure mode and a future validation discipline; it does not claim a solved transformation for this particular input.

# Trigger and scope in heterogeneous trajectory demos

A sparse-ray demo set may include both an unchanged configuration and one or more transformed configurations. Treat the unchanged pair as positive evidence about the trigger: it rules out blanket extension of every sparse arrangement. Infer the trigger independently from the path geometry—eligible marker color(s), whether multiple markers launch paths, required relative alignment, and stopping behavior.

Do not transfer a salient marker selection from one example to a visually different test without a cross-demo relation. Enumerate candidate paths and compare complete changed masks, including preserved markers and untouched lookalikes. A valid rule must explain both the transformed and identity demos. Request another pair only when two explicit trigger/scope candidates predict different observable outcomes; otherwise fully integrate existing evidence first.

After an incorrect prediction, discard the complete generator and revisit trigger, path direction, color, multiplicity, and scope rather than making a cosmetic coordinate tweak.

# Multi-ray recovery after a wrong trajectory prediction

A sparse-grid demo set may contain both an unchanged motif and a larger transformed motif. Treat identity as negative evidence about the trigger, not as an irrelevant example. Compare geometry, marker colors, and relative placements to determine what activates a transformation.

When the transformed example shows multiple trajectories, record each seed, color, direction vector, and stopping boundary separately. Do not infer that one salient color launches the only ray: test whether several marker groups launch distinct, simultaneous rays. Check all changed cells and untouched lookalikes in every demo.

After an incorrect output, reject the whole generator. Reconsider the launch condition and ray family rather than shifting a start point or submitting a one-ray subset. For the test, independently enumerate supported paths, preserve original markers, prevent unsupported overwrites, and validate boundaries. Request another demo only if its likely geometry would discriminate explicit competing launch/scope hypotheses.

# Post-error: test the full trajectory family

In a sparse-marker task, an initial one-color/template-style prediction was rejected even though the demo showed a marker-like structure changing. The demo's short changed portion was not sufficient to justify copying only that mask onto the most conspicuous test motif. Reassess activation and trajectory family independently: an identity example constrains when the operation triggers, while a transformed example may show simultaneous rays from several marker groups. Record each seed/color, direction, endpoint, and preserved intersection; project only paths supported by complete demo diffs. After an incorrect submission, discard the full generator rather than adding omitted rays or toggling a few cells without cross-demo evidence. This session's evidence did not establish a final rule, so this is a validation caution, not a solved-task recipe.

Before another demo request, specify competing trigger/trajectory hypotheses and the precise observation that would distinguish them.

# Underconstrained sparse-marker rays

A sparse input plus one short output trace may tempt the solver to infer a ray direction, launch marker, or stopping behavior. These are separate hypotheses: record exact seed coordinates and every changed coordinate, then test alternative directions, anchors, and scope against the whole demo. If multiple distinct generators fit the first pair, use a demo request to distinguish them before projecting any paths onto a differently shaped test grid. A plausible-looking ray is not validated merely because it can be drawn from a marker. Preserve original markers and off-path cells unless demonstrated otherwise.
